items.description: Nuclear heating power of a limiter tile is the rate at which nuclear energy is deposited within one limiter tile by neutron interactions and associated primary and secondary gamma-ray absorption.
items.documentation: Nuclear heating power of a limiter tile is the rate at which nuclear energy is deposited within one limiter tile by nuclear radiation transport and interactions in the tile material. It is a scalar heating-power contribution assigned to the material volume of that tile. The volume-integrated relation to the local nuclear power density is $$ P_{\mathrm{nuc},t} = \int_{V_t} q_{\mathrm{nuc}}(\mathbf{x}) \, dV $$ where $P_{\mathrm{nuc},t}$ is the nuclear heating power of the limiter tile, $V_t$ is the material volume occupied by the limiter tile, $q_{\mathrm{nuc}}(\mathbf{x})$ is the [nuclear power density of the limiter tile](name:nuclear_power_density_of_limiter_tile) at spatial position $\mathbf{x}$, and $dV$ is the differential volume element. The quantity applies to a single limiter tile and is aggregated over the whole material volume of that tile. It includes energy deposition from neutron interactions and absorption of primary and secondary gamma radiation within the tile material; deposition outside the tile is outside its scope. It is not the total nuclear energy deposited over a time interval, not a wall-total nuclear heating power, and not a non-nuclear heat load such as charged-particle, surface photon, ohmic, chemical, or coolant heat transfer. It is distinct from [nuclear heating power of a breeder blanket shield](name:nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_shield), which refers to nuclear heating in a different structural component. The nuclear energy deposited in the limiter tile over a time interval is the time integral of this power; this standard name denotes the deposition rate itself, not that time-integrated energy.

items.name: electron_density_at_outboard_midplane
items.description: Electron particle number density at the low-field-side intersection of a magnetic flux surface with the equatorial midplane.
items.documentation: Electron number density at the outboard midplane is the local density of the electron population at the low-field-side intersection of a specified magnetic flux surface with the equatorial midplane. It is the electron-specific member of density_at_outboard_midplane. At that location, the density is defined by the zeroth velocity-space moment $$ n_e(R,\phi,Z)=\int f_e(R,\phi,Z,\mathbf{v})\,d^3\mathbf{v} $$ where $n_e$ is electron number density, $f_e$ is the electron velocity-distribution function, $\mathbf{v}$ is velocity, and $d^3\mathbf{v}$ is the velocity-space volume element. The position is described in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. This quantity counts electrons only and is distinct from total particle density and from electron density evaluated at the magnetic axis.

items.name: normalized_collisionality
items.description: Dimensionless ratio of a specified interspecies collision frequency to the characteristic streaming, transit, or bounce frequency used for the plasma population.
items.documentation:
This collisionality measures the strength of interspecies collisional relaxation relative to collisionless motion along magnetic-field trajectories. $$ 
u_{ab}^{*} =  rac{
u_{ab}}{\omega_{\mathrm{char}}} $$ where $
u_{ab}$ is the collision frequency between species $a$ and $b$, and $\omega_{\mathrm{char}}$ is the relevant characteristic streaming, transit, or bounce angular frequency; both quantities have reciprocal-time units. The denominator must be interpreted according to the selected orbit or motion class, so this quantity is distinct from the collision frequency itself. It generalizes the population-specific electron collisionality and complements collisionality at the pedestal top when the characteristic frequency is evaluated there.

items.name: runaway_electron_source_rate_due_to_hot_tail
items.description: Hot-tail runaway-electron source rate is the production of runaway electrons per unit volume and time from a suprathermal tail surviving rapid cooling of the bulk electrons.
items.documentation: Hot-tail runaway-electron source rate quantifies production of runaway electrons from the high-energy electron tail that survives rapid cooling of the bulk population. These tail electrons relax collisionally more slowly than the bulk cools, allowing some to enter the regime where electric-field acceleration overcomes collisional drag. The hot-tail contribution to runaway-electron density evolution is defined by $$ S_{\mathrm{ht}} = \left.\frac{\partial n_{\mathrm{RE}}}{\partial t}\right|_{\mathrm{hot\text{-}tail}} $$ where $S_{\mathrm{ht}}$ is the volumetric hot-tail production rate, $n_{\mathrm{RE}}$ is the [runaway-electron number density](name:runaway_electron_density), and $t$ is time. The restriction on the derivative selects only production through the hot-tail mechanism. This source counts electrons entering the runaway population, not all suprathermal electrons. It excludes generation through other mechanisms, transport, and losses, so it is not the full time derivative of runaway-electron density. It contributes to the [total runaway-electron source rate](name:total_runaway_electron_source_rate), which sums all active generation mechanisms. The [volume-averaged hot-tail runaway-electron source rate](name:volume_averaged_runaway_electron_source_rate_due_to_hot_tail) is this same volumetric source integrated over the plasma volume and divided by that volume.

items.name: inner_squareness_of_flux_surface
items.description: Dimensionless Luce shape coefficient quantifying how much the high-field-side (inner) corners of a nested magnetic flux surface deviate from a reference ellipse; positive values indicate a boxier corner, negative values a more diamond-like or indented corner.
items.documentation: The inner squareness of a flux surface is the dimensionless Luce (2013) shape coefficient that characterizes how much the high-field-side (inboard, smaller major radius) corners of a nested toroidal magnetic flux surface depart from a reference ellipse sharing the same center, horizontal half-width, and [elongation](name:elongation_of_flux_surface). It is the inboard counterpart within the [squareness_of_flux_surface](name:squareness_of_flux_surface) family, complementing the outboard variants [upper_outer_squareness_of_flux_surface](name:upper_outer_squareness_of_flux_surface) and [lower_outer_squareness_of_flux_surface](name:lower_outer_squareness_of_flux_surface). This parent quantity abstracts over the quadrant-resolved coefficients [upper_inner_squareness_of_flux_surface](name:upper_inner_squareness_of_flux_surface) and [lower_inner_squareness_of_flux_surface](name:lower_inner_squareness_of_flux_surface), which independently describe the upper and lower high-field-side corners. The coefficient $\zeta$ enters the parametric flux-surface shape model as an additional harmonic beyond elongation $\kappa$ and triangularity $\delta$, evaluated at the high-field-side corners of the poloidal cross-section in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height. A value of zero recovers the reference ellipse precisely; deviations capture corner shaping not expressible through $\kappa$ and $\delta$ alone. The inner squareness is inferred from equilibrium reconstruction by fitting closed flux-surface contours to a multi-parameter shape model. Asymmetry between upper and lower inner quadrants can arise in vertically asymmetric or diverted configurations, motivating the quadrant-resolved child quantities.

items.name: electron_pressure
items.description: Electron kinetic pressure is one-third of the trace of the velocity-space stress, covering thermal, suprathermal, and combined populations.
items.documentation: Electron kinetic pressure is the isotropic scalar measure of momentum flux generated by random electron motion about the population mean velocity. It may describe a suprathermal component, a thermal component, or their combined electron population. The defining pressure is $$ p_e = \frac{m_e}{3}\int \lvert \mathbf{v}-\mathbf{u}_e\rvert^2 f_e(\mathbf{v})\,d^3v $$ where $p_e$ is the electron kinetic pressure, $m_e$ is the electron mass, $\mathbf{v}$ is an individual electron velocity, $\mathbf{u}_e$ is the mean velocity of the represented electron population, $f_e(\mathbf{v})$ is its velocity distribution, and $d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume element. At parent scope, the quantity applies to a selected thermal or suprathermal electron population or to their full aggregate. Aggregation is over the represented electrons in velocity space, not over ion or neutral species; the full aggregate combines disjoint thermal and suprathermal contributions. This quantity is the trace-based scalar reduction of the electron kinetic stress and does not specify a directional pressure-tensor component. An anisotropic electron stress is therefore represented here only through its trace, while ion pressure, neutral pressure, and individual tensor components are excluded. The [fast-electron pressure contribution](name:fast_electron_pressure) is the suprathermal component within this common kinetic-pressure concept. The [total electron pressure](name:total_electron_pressure) is the aggregate over the designated thermal and suprathermal electron populations and equals their sum when those components are disjoint.

items.name: x_second_measurement_direction_unit_vector_of_strain_gauge
items.description: Signed direction cosine of a strain gage’s second measurement direction along the x axis of the right-handed Cartesian (x, y, z) frame.
items.documentation: The quantity is the x projection of the unit vector defining a strain gage’s second measurement direction. It describes orientation, not the gage’s spatial location or its first measurement direction. The direction cosine is defined by: $$ d_{2x} = \hat{\mathbf d}_2 \cdot \hat{\mathbf x} $$ where $\hat{\mathbf d}_2$ is the unit vector along the second measurement direction and $\hat{\mathbf x}$ is the x-axis unit vector in the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ frame. Together with the y direction cosine of the second measurement direction and z direction cosine of the second measurement direction, it specifies that direction. It is distinct from the [x coordinate of the sensor attachment point](name:x_coordinate_of_sensor_attachment_point), which locates the gage rather than defining its orientation. Sign convention: Positive when the second measurement direction has a component along increasing x in the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ frame.

items.name: radial_effective_electron_diffusivity
items.description: Effective coefficient relating the radial diffusive flux of electron particles to the radial gradient of electron number density in edge-plasma transport.
items.documentation: Effective coefficient relating the radial diffusive flux of electron particles to the radial gradient of electron number density is the scalar Fickian closure coefficient for radial electron particle diffusion in the edge plasma. It describes the diffusive, cross-field radial part of electron particle transport. The radial diffusive electron particle flux is related to the radial density gradient by $$ \Gamma_{e,r}^{\mathrm{diff}} = -D_{e,r}^{\mathrm{eff}}\,\frac{\partial n_e}{\partial r} $$ where $\Gamma_{e,r}^{\mathrm{diff}}$ is the radial diffusive electron particle flux, $D_{e,r}^{\mathrm{eff}}$ is this effective radial electron diffusivity, $n_e$ is the [electron number density](name:electron_number_density), and $r$ is the radial transport coordinate. The scope is electron particles in the edge plasma and the radial component of the diffusive particle-flux closure. It excludes the convective or advective part of electron particle flux, particle sources and sinks, parallel transport along the magnetic field, and the total electron particle flux. It is the radial member of the direction-dependent [effective electron diffusivity](name:effective_electron_diffusivity). The broader [electron diffusion coefficient](name:electron_diffusion_coefficient) denotes electron particle diffusion without the radial effective-component restriction, while the radial electron diffusion coefficient denotes the corresponding radial coefficient when the effective-closure distinction is not made. With the minus sign in the defining relation, a positive $D_{e,r}^{\mathrm{eff}}$ produces diffusive electron particle flux down the gradient of $n_e$; an effective negative value represents an up-gradient flux contribution in the same closure.

items.name: neon_prefill_count
items.description: Neon prefill count is the total amount of neutral neon (Ne) introduced before plasma breakdown, expressed as an equivalent-electron count with 10 equivalent electrons per atom.
items.documentation: Neon prefill count is the total amount of neutral neon (Ne) introduced during the prefill phase before plasma breakdown, expressed as an equivalent-electron count. Each neutral neon atom contributes 10 equivalent electrons. The equivalent-electron count is defined by $$ N_{e,\mathrm{eq}}^{\mathrm{Ne,prefill}} = Z_{\mathrm{Ne}}N_{\mathrm{Ne,prefill}} = 10N_{\mathrm{Ne,prefill}} = \int_{t_0}^{t_{\mathrm{bd}}}10\dot{N}_{\mathrm{Ne}}(t)\,dt $$ where $N_{e,\mathrm{eq}}^{\mathrm{Ne,prefill}}$ is the neon equivalent-electron count and $N_{\mathrm{Ne,prefill}}$ is the accumulated neutral-neon atom count, both pure counts; $Z_{\mathrm{Ne}}=10$ is the atomic number of neon; $\dot{N}_{\mathrm{Ne}}$ is the neutral-neon atom introduction rate in atoms s$^{-1}$; and $t_0$ and $t_{\mathrm{bd}}$ are the prefill start and plasma-breakdown times, with $t$ in s. This quantity includes only neutral neon introduced before breakdown and excludes wall recycling, neutral-beam or pellet fueling, later gas injection, and retained or ionized inventory. The equivalent-electron convention is an accounting normalization based on neutral atomic composition, not a statement that the gas is fully ionized during prefill. It is the neon component of [prefill_count](name:prefill_count); [accumulated_neon_count](name:accumulated_neon_count) represents distinct post-breakdown accumulation, while [argon_prefill_count](name:argon_prefill_count) applies the same convention to a different noble gas.

items.name: radiated_power_of_breeder_blanket_module
items.description: Radiated power associated with a single breeder blanket module, abstracting over plasma electromagnetic power incident on the module surface, the reflected portion, and the absorbed portion retained as a module heat load as distinct radiation energy-budget components.
items.documentation: Radiated power of a breeder blanket module quantifies the rate at which plasma electromagnetic emission, chiefly bremsstrahlung continuum and atomic line radiation, is assigned to the module-level radiation channel. It is the umbrella scalar for the incident photon power crossing onto the module surface and the absorbed photon power retained after surface reflection, represented by [incident_radiated_power_of_breeder_blanket_module](name:incident_radiated_power_of_breeder_blanket_module) and [absorbed_radiated_power_of_breeder_blanket_module](name:absorbed_radiated_power_of_breeder_blanket_module). The radiated-power component for a single module is defined by integrating the corresponding radiative surface energy flux over the module surface: $$ P_{\mathrm{rad},c} = \int_{A_m} \Phi_{\mathrm{rad},c}\, dA,\qquad c \in \{\mathrm{inc},\mathrm{abs}\} $$ where $P_{\mathrm{rad},c}$ is the module-level radiated-power component in watts, $A_m$ is the module plasma-facing surface, $dA$ is a surface element, $\Phi_{\mathrm{rad},\mathrm{inc}}$ is the incident photon energy flux density onto that surface, and $\Phi_{\mathrm{rad},\mathrm{abs}}$ is the retained photon energy flux density after reflection. The incident and absorbed components are related by the surface-reflection balance $P_{\mathrm{rad},\mathrm{abs}} = P_{\mathrm{rad},\mathrm{inc}} - P_{\mathrm{rad},\mathrm{ref}}$, equivalently $P_{\mathrm{rad},\mathrm{abs}} = (1-\mathcal{R})P_{\mathrm{rad},\mathrm{inc}}$ for an effective reflectance $\mathcal{R}$. The parent quantity is not a sum of incident and absorbed terms; it identifies the module radiation channel, while the component qualifier identifies which surface-budget term is represented. Neutron surface loads, volumetric nuclear energy deposition, auxiliary heating, and thermal radiation emitted by the module itself are outside this radiated-power channel; the absorbed part contributes to thermal_power_of_breeder_blanket_module within [power_of_breeder_blanket_module](name:power_of_breeder_blanket_module).

items.name: second_local_tangential_coordinate_of_optical_element
items.description: Signed position of a fiber center or outline vertex at an optical element along its second local tangential axis, measured relative to the element-local origin.
items.documentation: The second local tangential coordinate locates an individual fiber center or outline vertex at an optical element. It belongs to the element-local Cartesian frame $(X_1, X_2)$, where $X_1$ and $X_2$ denote coordinates along the first and second local tangents, respectively. The coordinate is defined by $$ X_2 = (\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}_0)\cdot\hat{\mathbf{t}}_2 $$ where $\mathbf{r}$ is the position vector of the specified point, $\mathbf{r}_0$ is the position vector of the element-local origin, and $\hat{\mathbf{t}}_2$ is the unit vector along the positive second local tangent. Each value describes one fiber center or outline vertex, not an average over those points. Fiber-center coordinates locate individual fibers, whereas outline coordinates locate boundary vertices; neither denotes an element width or a surface-normal displacement. The second tangent is object-local and is not prescribed to be vertical. For fiber-center positions in a fiber bundle, the [first local tangential coordinate of the fiber bundle] supplies the complementary coordinate of the same center in the local plane. Sign convention: Positive when the displacement from the element-local origin has a positive projection onto the designated second local tangential axis.

items.name: torque_density
items.description: Local vector rate of net angular-momentum transfer per unit volume to or from plasma, with population-, orbit-class-, mechanism-, and component-specific forms.
items.documentation: Torque density is the local vector rate at which angular momentum is transferred to or from a specified plasma content, expressed per unit volume. It retains the complete torque-vector direction unless a component-specific form is selected. The defining relation is $$ \boldsymbol{\tau} = \left(\frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\ell}}{\partial t}\right)_{\mathrm{transfer}} $$ where $\boldsymbol{\tau}$ is the torque-density vector and $\boldsymbol{\ell}$ is the angular-momentum density of the selected plasma content. The transfer term is net over the mechanisms and populations included by the specific quantity. Population- and orbit-class-resolved instances include [ion torque density](name:ion_torque_density), [neutral torque density](name:neutral_torque_density), and trapped or passing contributions; [toroidal torque density](name:toroidal_torque_density) is the corresponding directional component. Sign convention: Positive when the torque vector points along the corresponding positive direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ basis; the toroidal component is positive when it increases angular momentum in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

items.name: volume_integrated_particle_source_rate
items.description: Volume-integrated particle source rate is the net number of particles added to a specified distribution per unit time by a source contribution over the plasma volume.
items.documentation: Volume-integrated particle source rate is the net particle-number input to a specified particle distribution from a given source contribution, integrated over the plasma volume. The defining volume integral is $$ S(t) = \int_V s_p(\mathbf{x},t)\,d^3x $$ where $S$ is the volume-integrated particle source rate, $t$ is time, $V$ is the plasma volume, $\mathbf{x}$ is physical position, $d^3x$ is the volume element, and $s_p$ is the local net particle source rate per physical volume. For a kinetic source term, $s_p$ is its velocity-space integral, the particle-number moment. The rate applies to the species and population represented by the specified distribution. Volume integration does not imply summation over other distributions, species, or source mechanisms. For a distribution-function-driven contribution, it is the volume integral of the [particle source rate due to distribution-function-driven processes](name:particle_source_rate_due_to_distribution_function_driven), not its volume average. No restriction to thermal particles or thermalization is implied. When the contribution describes thermalization, it counts transfer from fast particles into the thermal background, rather than particle creation in the combined populations; reverse transfer constitutes a sink for the thermal population. Sign convention: Positive when the source contribution adds particles to the specified distribution; negative when it removes particles.
